props.title: Circuitry Man
props.initialSlug: Future noir: cyborg smuggler races for survival

sections.content: Circuitry Man (1990) emerged during cyberpunk's direct-to-video golden age, riding the neon wave that Blade Runner (1982) sparked. This low-budget gem stars Jim Metzler as Danner, a smuggler trafficking illegal computer chips in a post-apocalyptic world where brain-enhancing electronics are the new drug trade. The film's grimy aesthetic and underground tech culture perfectly capture the DIY spirit of early 90s sci-fi, sharing DNA with contemporaries like Hardware (1990) and Nemesis (1992).

sections.content: Director Steven Lovy crafted a distinctly analog vision of the future that feels more authentic than many bigger-budget contemporaries. The practical effects and physical props create a tangible world of jerry-rigged technology that predicted our current modding and maker culture. This approach connects it to other hands-on sci-fi like Death Machine (1994) and Split Second (1992), where the future feels worn and jerry-rigged rather than sleek and corporate.

The film's themes of body modification and chemical enhancement proved remarkably prescient, predating similar ideas in Johnny Mnemonic (1995) and Strange Days (1995). Vernon Wells delivers a memorably unhinged performance as Plughead, a villain who literally feeds on electricity - a character that would influence countless techno-horror antagonists to follow. sections.content: While Circuitry Man never achieved mainstream success, its influence can be traced through later cyberpunk works. The idea of chip-running and neural enhancement would become major themes in Ghost in the Shell (1995) and the tabletop RPG Shadowrun. The film even spawned its own sequel, Circuitry Man II: Plughead Rewired (1994), though it failed to capture the scrappy charm of the original.
